analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and repeals its authorizing law.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau was introduced by one senator with a single cosponsor and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the agency created after the 2008 financial crisis to police mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, and debt collection on behalf of consumers. It does this by repealing the 2010 law that created the Bureau and restoring the older laws that existed before it. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there with no action.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, debt collectors, and other consumer financial companies would have been freed from the CFPB's rulemaking, supervision, and enforcement. The agency that had returned billions to consumers for improper fees and lending practices would no longer exist, and consumer financial products would go back to being policed, as before 2010, by banking regulators who also supervise the same banks.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the law that established the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, thereby eliminating the agency entirely.
Revives or restores the provisions of law that the 2010 Act had amended or repealed, as if it had never been enacted, returning consumer financial regulation to its pre-2010 structure.

Under that pre-2010 structure, consumer products like mortgages and credit cards were overseen by banking regulators rather than a dedicated consumer agency, meaning the same regulators supervised the banks they were policing.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who use mortgages, credit cards, student loans, payday loans, and credit reports would bear the cost: no dedicated agency would write rules against deceptive or abusive practices, supervise lenders for compliance, or take enforcement actions and obtain refunds when consumers are cheated. Protections would be scattered among regulators whose primary mandate is the safety of the banks themselves.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Act revives or restores the pre-2010 provisions of law, dissolving the single dedicated consumer regulator and returning its functions to the scattered pre-Dodd-Frank framework.

The strongest good-faith objection supporters of repeal would raise — that the Bureau has a single director and is funded by the Federal Reserve rather than by congressional appropriations, making it less accountable than typical agencies — addresses how the Bureau is run, not whether consumers lose the protections themselves; this bill did not reform the Bureau's structure but eliminated it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows almost entirely to regulated financial firms, in the form of removal of a dedicated regulator, while the cost falls on consumers, who would lose the agency responsible for rules, supervision, and enforcement across mortgages, credit cards, and lending. The bill offered no replacement consumer protections; it simply restored the pre-2010 legal landscape.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on July 21, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill had a single cosponsor, a Republican, and no Democratic support.
No further action was ever taken: the Banking Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and its last recorded action was the referral on the day of introduction.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill ever receiving a floor vote, so the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 and the Bureau it created remained in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: the CFPB survived, because a bill to eliminate it never advanced past a committee referral. Banks, payday lenders, and other firms seeking repeal gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Texas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Repeal CFPB Act to eliminate the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection.

for.name: Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; because the bill never reached a vote, no roll-call record exists, but the sponsorship pattern was entirely one-sided by party.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: Repeal would have removed the dedicated regulator that writes consumer protection rules, supervises lenders for compliance, and brings enforcement actions — including refunds — against these firms. Their gain from deregulation comes directly at the cost of consumers' protections.

These lenders were among the most frequent targets of CFPB scrutiny; eliminating the Bureau would have removed the agency positioned to restrict or police their lending practices. The saving for lenders comes from practices consumers would no longer have a regulator challenging.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: The CFPB is the primary federal enforcer over debt collection and credit reporting practices; repeal would have removed that oversight. The industry's benefit would come at the expense of consumers disputing debts or credit report errors.
